content: Tanning addiction is a condition in which an individual develops a physical and/or psychological dependency on sunbathing or the use of tanning beds. The exact mechanism underlying this addiction remains unknown. In 2005, dermatologists conducted a study that revealed frequent tanners often lose control over their tanning habits, exhibiting behaviors similar to those seen in individuals addicted to substances like nicotine or alcohol. Biochemical evidence suggests that tanning addiction may be linked to the release of opioids in the body during tanning. A 2006 study demonstrated that when frequent tanners were given an endorphin-blocking medication, they experienced severe withdrawal symptoms. In contrast, individuals who tanned infrequently did not exhibit withdrawal symptoms under the same conditions. The term tanorexia is often used to describe a condition in which a person engages in excessive sun tanning or overuses artificial tanning methods, such as tanning beds, in an effort to achieve a darker skin tone. This behavior is driven by the perception that their natural skin tone is unacceptably pale. While tanorexia and tanning addiction share similarities and may overlap, they are distinct conditions. The term tanorexia is not widely recognized or accepted by the medical community and is often considered slang. It was coined in reference to anorexia nervosa, a psychiatric disorder characterized by an obsessive fear of gaining weight, distorted body image, and dangerously low body weight. The comparison to anorexia nervosa is based on the idea of a distorted self-perception. Just as individuals with anorexia nervosa may perceive themselves as overweight despite being underweight, individuals with tanorexia may believe their skin is too pale even when it is already dark. The term tanorexia has also been likened to the colloquial practice of adding the suffix -oholic to describe excessive behaviors, such as chocoholic or shopaholic. Severe cases of tanorexia can pose significant health risks. In extreme cases, tanorexia may be associated with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a mental health condition characterized by obsessive and compulsive preoccupation with perceived flaws in one’s appearance. Individuals with BDD often exhibit a distorted body image, similar to those with anorexia nervosa. For example, while individuals with anorexia may see themselves as fat despite being underweight, individuals with tanorexia may perceive their skin as pale even when it is already dark. Although tanorexia is not officially recognized as a medical diagnosis, reported symptoms include intense anxiety when unable to tan, competitive behavior among peers to achieve the darkest tan, and persistent dissatisfaction with one’s skin tone. Affected individuals may be convinced that their complexion is lighter than it actually is, leading to chronic frustration.
